items.title: How long photons take to escape the Sun
items.claim: A photon generated in the Sun's core takes how long, on average, to reach the surface?
items.reveal_title: Tens of thousands of years through a dense plasma
items.reveal:
The radiative zone is so opaque that photons random-walk outward. Mitalas and Sills (1992) modelled the escape time at about 10,000 to 170,000 years depending on assumptions.

Once free, the photon reaches Earth in about 8 minutes 20 seconds.
items.why: The dramatic part of a photon's journey is hidden inside its source, not its trip across space.

items.title: Why we infer dark matter
items.claim: Vera Rubin and Kent Ford in the 1970s measured spiral galaxy rotation curves. What did they find?

options.text: Rotation slowed at the edges as Keplerian dynamics would predict
Rotation stayed roughly flat at large radii, implying more mass than visible matter accounted for

items.reveal_title: Flat rotation curves implied invisible mass
items.reveal:
Rubin and Ford's 1970s observations confirmed earlier hints (Zwicky 1933 on cluster dynamics).

Current cosmological models attribute roughly 27% of the universe's mass-energy budget to dark matter, 68% to dark energy and around 5% to baryonic matter.
items.why: Most of what controls galactic dynamics is something we cannot see directly.

items.title: How the CMB was found
items.claim: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson discovered the cosmic microwave background in 1964 while working at Bell Labs. What were they originally trying to do?

options.text: Refining a horn antenna for radio communications, with the persistent noise traced to a cosmic source

items.reveal_title: An accidental discovery in a communications lab
items.reveal:
Penzias and Wilson were eliminating noise sources, including pigeon droppings inside the antenna. The Princeton group nearby was independently looking for exactly this signal.

Nobel Prize 1978 went to Penzias and Wilson.
items.why: Major cosmological evidence has come from accident as often as from targeted experiment.

items.title: Lemaitre before Hubble
items.claim: Hubble's 1929 paper reported a relationship between galaxy distance and redshift, indicating expansion. Who derived the relationship two years earlier?
items.reveal:
Lemaitre's 1927 paper in Annales de la Societe Scientifique de Bruxelles included an estimate of the expansion rate.

The IAU resolved in 2018 to refer to the law as the Hubble-Lemaitre Law.
items.why: Language and journal of publication shape who gets credited for foundational results.

items.title: Why Pluto was reclassified
items.claim: The IAU's 2006 definition of 'planet' has three conditions: it orbits the Sun, has enough mass for hydrostatic equilibrium, and what?
items.reveal_title: 'Cleared the neighbourhood' is the criterion Pluto fails
items.reveal:
Pluto orbits within the Kuiper Belt with comparable bodies (notably Eris). The IAU created the 'dwarf planet' category.

Ceres in the asteroid belt is also a dwarf planet under the definition.
items.why: Scientific categories sometimes change to track the evidence rather than vice versa.

items.title: The first confirmed exoplanets
items.claim: The first exoplanets confirmed orbited an unusual host. What was it?

options.text: A pulsar (PSR B1257+12), with the discovery announced in 1992

items.reveal_title: Pulsar planets, three years before 51 Pegasi b
items.reveal:
Aleksander Wolszczan and Dale Frail confirmed planets around the millisecond pulsar PSR B1257+12 in 1992.

Mayor and Queloz's 51 Pegasi b (1995) was the first around a sunlike star and won the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics.
items.why: Public memory often centres on the second discovery if the first occurs in an exotic setting.

items.title: JWST launch and arrival
items.claim: The James Webb Space Telescope launched on 25 December 2021. About how long to reach its operating point at L2?

options.text: About 30 days for L2 insertion; first science images released July 2022

items.reveal_title: About a month to L2; six months of commissioning before first science
items.reveal:
JWST inserted into L2 orbit on 24 January 2022. The first science images were released 12 July 2022.

The Sun-Earth L2 point lies about 1.5 million km from Earth.
items.why: Headline 'launch day' obscures months of staging required to make a telescope work.

items.title: Voyager 1 entering interstellar space
items.claim: Voyager 1 launched in 1977. When did NASA conclude it had crossed into interstellar space?

options.text: Around August 2012, confirmed by NASA in 2013

items.reveal:
Plasma density measurements from the Plasma Wave Subsystem confirmed the crossing.

Voyager 1 still transmits data; its plutonium power source will deplete in the mid-2020s to early 2030s.
items.why: Defining 'interstellar' requires a physical boundary, the heliopause, not a fixed distance.

items.title: The Milky Way and Andromeda
items.claim: Andromeda (M31) is moving toward the Milky Way at about 110 km/s. When are current models predicting first close passage?
items.reveal_title: Around 4.5 billion years, plus or minus
items.reveal:
Cox and Loeb (2008) predicted a close passage around 4.5 billion years from now, with full merger over subsequent billions of years.

Gaia data have refined Andromeda's tangential motion since.
items.why: Galactic-scale events follow timescales that dwarf human history.

items.title: First imaged black hole
items.claim: The Event Horizon Telescope released the first image of a supermassive black hole in 2019. Which one?

options.text: Sagittarius A* in the Milky Way
The black hole at the centre of M87, around 53 million light-years away
A solar-mass black hole in Cygnus

items.reveal_title: M87* came first; Sagittarius A* followed in 2022
items.reveal:
EHT's M87* image released 10 April 2019; Sagittarius A* image released 12 May 2022. M87* is roughly 6.5 billion solar masses; Sagittarius A* is around 4 million.

EHT combines radio telescopes on multiple continents to create an Earth-sized aperture.
items.why: Imaging the largest objects in the universe required a planet-sized synthetic instrument.

items.title: What the universe expands into
items.claim: When cosmologists say the universe is expanding, what is the most accurate description of where it expands to?

options.text: The metric of space itself increases distances between unbound objects; there is no external 'outside'

items.reveal_title: Expansion is of the metric, not into a container
items.reveal:
General relativity describes the metric of space evolving with time. The FLRW metric encodes this expansion.

Gravitationally bound systems (galaxies, the Local Group) are not expanding with the cosmic flow.
items.why: Cosmology requires letting go of everyday intuitions about space as a fixed stage.

items.title: Lunar samples returned
items.claim: How much lunar material did the six Apollo missions return to Earth in total?
items.reveal:
Apollo 11 returned about 22 kg; later missions returned larger samples. Soviet Luna robotic missions returned around 0.3 kg.

China's Chang'e 5 (2020) returned around 1.7 kg.
items.why: Sample-return missions remain extremely costly per gram delivered, shaping research priorities.
